parts.note: an account is a bill to be paid, and the talking is done down a phone line, so this is the invoice for calls

explanation.surface: Someone demands an explanation for all the chatter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Account for' looks like 'explain', but it is a noun phrase: the account (bill) covering all the talking.
explanation.definitionFit: The periodic invoice from a phone company charges for every call made.

clue.text: Are moving home, it must be serious

indicators.note: moving suggests the letters of the word are shift about into a new order

parts.note: a nest is a bird's home

explanation.surface: Moving house is a solemn business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges ARE into EAR, then NEST follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnest and serious are synonyms, both meaning sincere and not joking.

parts.note: the sea goes out after it has risen at high tide; this is what the tide does next

explanation.surface: Someone leaves after a pay rise.
explanation.definitionFit: The tide flows out, or recedes, after coming in to high water.

parts.note: to strike is to hit
a back is a defensive player in football or rugby

explanation.surface: Someone gets even by thumping a sportsman.
explanation.definitionFit: To retaliate is to answer an attack with a counter-blow.

parts.note: the part of a newspaper given over to critics' write-ups of plays and books

explanation.surface: A part of a publication is set aside for critics.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics' write-ups of a play or film are called its press notices.

clue.text: Lines at last for the annoying child

indicators.note: last says the word at is placed at the end of the charade

parts.note: BR is British Rail, whose railway lines are a crossword staple

explanation.surface: Railway lines are finally the destination for a tiresome youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: BR, short for British Rail, the former national railway, gives the 'Lines'.
explanation.definitionFit: A brat is a badly behaved, irritating youngster.

parts.note: not the guitar genre but music to which an infant is rocked to sleep

explanation.surface: A genre of loud guitar music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock music' reads as the genre; here 'Rock' is a verb, what a parent does to a cradle.
explanation.definitionFit: A gentle song sung to soothe a baby to sleep while rocking it.

clue.text: Rome's source for investors looking for a return

definitions.text: Rome's source for investors looking for a return

parts.words: Rome's source for investors looking for a return
parts.note: tourists toss coins into a famous Roman fountain so that they will come back to the city

explanation.surface: An Italian fount of finance for investors hoping for a profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investors' and 'return' suggest finance; the 'investors' are tourists throwing coins and the 'return' is a trip back to Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says a coin thrown into this Baroque Roman fountain guarantees the thrower's return to the city.

indicators.note: gathering suggests the letters of the two words are collected together and reassembled

explanation.surface: Crossing a path, one collects precious finds.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of TRAVERSE and ROUTE together rearrange into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoard of buried gold or silver found by chance counts as treasure of unknown ownership.

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the word arbiter is remade into new order

explanation.surface: A style judge from Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion arbiter' reads as a style guru; 'Fashion' is a verb working on ARBITER. Welsh rarebit is cheese on toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh rarebit is a savoury dish of melted cheese on toast.

clue.text: Vessel churning up water left and right

indicators.note: churning up stirs the letters of water and the two side letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A boat thrashes the sea about on both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'churning up' mixes WATER with L and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishing boat that drags a large net through the sea.

indicators.note: changing indicates the letters of ever are altered into another order

explanation.surface: Breezes are forever shifting direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Meteorologists use this verb for a wind shifting clockwise in direction; the noun follows.

definitions.meaning: a game or contest between two sides
small sticks for lighting fires are sold in boxes

explanation.definitionFit: A sporting contest, and also the small striking stick sold by the boxful.

parts.note: a crack is a joke, as is a gag

indicators.note: to start with means take only the opening letter of almonds

explanation.surface: Instructions for cracking almonds first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' and 'almonds' set a nutty scene, but 'Nuts' means crazy and 'crack' is a quip.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaga and nuts are both slang for mad or senile.

clue.text: Come out with me again and have a drink

indicators.note: again says the reduced piece appears a second time
out with me means the word me is removed from come

explanation.surface: An invitation to a date and a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: COME with ME taken out leaves CO; 'again' doubles it to COCO, and A ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot chocolate-flavoured beverage made from cacao powder.

indicators.note: a variety of the word Hardy is a different arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A tough strain of fearsome beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective or the novelist Thomas Hardy; it is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The many-headed serpent of Greek myth slain by Heracles.

clue.text: Left 'ock damaged by tuft of horsehair

indicators.note: damaged suggests the letters are knocked about into another order

explanation.surface: A horse's hock, dropping its H Cockney-style, is hurt and leaves a tuft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ock is hock with the H dropped, as in Cockney speech; LEFT and OCK are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuft of hair behind a horse's hoof joint gives its name to the joint itself.

parts.note: a request to cite the phrase someone uses when doubting what they hear

explanation.surface: An instruction to cite a sceptical remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A colloquial retort meaning 'I don't believe you' or 'that's only your opinion'.

clue.text: All the same, it suits some people

definitions.meaning: a suit of clothing worn by soldiers, nurses or schoolchildren

explanation.definitionFit: As adjective it means consistent and unvarying; as a noun it is the official outfit some groups wear.

clue.text: To some extent it's of Iran's making

indicators.note: making suggests the letters are built into a new form

parts.note: the possessive S is kept as a letter here

explanation.surface: Partly, Iran is responsible.
explanation.walkthrough: OF and IRANS are rearranged; the apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase means to the degree that, or as far as.

clue.text: He had his first signal success about the turn of the century

definitions.text: He had his first signal success about the turn of the century

parts.words: He had his first signal success about the turn of the century
parts.note: refers to the radio pioneer who sent a wireless signal across the Atlantic in 1901

explanation.surface: Someone first won notable acclaim around 1900.
explanation.walkthrough: 'signal success' reads as 'notable success'; it was literally a successful signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian inventor transmitted the first transatlantic radio message in December 1901.

clue.text: The sort of hat one may have to eat?

definitions.text: The sort of hat one may have to eat?

parts.words: The sort of hat one may have to eat?
parts.note: a flat-topped hat named after a savoury pastry, plus the idiom of eating your hat when wrong

explanation.surface: Which hat would one have to swallow after losing a bet?
explanation.walkthrough: To 'eat one's hat' is to admit being wrong; this hat shares its name with a meat pastry.
explanation.definitionFit: A low hat with a flat crown, named for its resemblance to a British meat pastry.

parts.note: to pan a play is to criticise it harshly
to long for something is to ache for it

explanation.surface: Run down a long sprint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dash' looks like a sprint; it means flair.
explanation.definitionFit: Dash and panache both mean flamboyant style and verve.

indicators.note: possibly signals that spy may be arranged differently

parts.note: chic means stylish or fashionable

explanation.surface: Perhaps a spy is watching a trendy clairvoyant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'medium' could be a size; here it is one who contacts spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: A medium claims to communicate with the dead, a clairvoyant gift.

definitions.meaning: to sample something is to try it out

explanation.definitionFit: Both a trial or examination and a verb meaning to try out.

indicators.note: out here means disordered, so the word burnt is set in another order

explanation.surface: Exhausted from pressure, someone is burnt out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burnt out' looks like a phrase; 'out' rearranges BURNT.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear the brunt is to take the main force or strain of something.

clue.text: He changes colour in Ryde, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps means the letters of Ryde could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Someone goes red in an Isle of Wight town.
explanation.walkthrough: Ryde is a town on the Isle of Wight off England's south coast; its letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who colours cloth with pigments.

clue.text: He's amongst the richest men in the land

indicators.note: amongst says the name lies among the letters of the following words

explanation.surface: A man counted among the wealthiest people in the country.
explanation.walkthrough: The name sits across 'thE RIChest'; 'men in the land' completes the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A common male given name, so a fair answer to 'He'.

clue.text: Juliet's town is just not on for her

indicators.note: not on means the letters of on are left out

parts.note: Shakespeare set Romeo and Juliet in Verona

explanation.surface: Juliet's home town is unfair to her.
explanation.walkthrough: VERONA without ON leaves a woman's name; 'just not on' reads as 'simply unacceptable'.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, so a woman referred to as 'her'.

clue.text: Conclude there's no place for the damned

parts.note: to conclude is to infer

explanation.surface: One deduces there is no room for lost souls.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante's name for Hell, the realm where the condemned suffer.

clue.text: He had an uncle and sisters on the stage

definitions.text: He had an uncle and sisters on the stage

parts.words: He had an uncle and sisters on the stage
parts.note: points to the Russian dramatist who wrote plays about an uncle and three sisters

explanation.surface: Someone has relatives who are actors.
explanation.walkthrough: The relatives are the plays Uncle Vanya and Three Sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian playwright wrote Uncle Vanya and Three Sisters.

parts.note: a marriage is a union or pairing, and a trial one is a warm-up game

explanation.surface: Living together before tying the knot.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'match' can be a marriage, so a trial one is a warm-up game.
explanation.definitionFit: A friendly game played as preparation rather than for points.
